title: You forgot
hook: when troubled, you've forgotten that each person's mind shares in the divine (Meditations 12.26)

segments.voice: Yesterday: all is opinion, the label we add to events, and the sailor rounding into calm water. Your line was in my power. Which label did you choose again? Day six hundred thirty-four.

You walk into the kitchen and stand there. Why did you come in? You knew a second ago. Everybody does this. Marcus Aurelius thought being upset is a lot like that kitchen moment: not that you never knew the truth, but that it slipped out of your hand on the way in. So in book twelve he writes himself a list. Not of new ideas, but of things he already knew and keeps forgetting the moment someone annoys him. It's one of the most honest pages in the book. Today: you forgot.
screen: `WHY DID I COME IN HERE?` → `NOT NEW IDEAS. OLD ONES, DROPPED.` → `YOU FORGOT.`

segments.voice: Meditations 12.26 opens, in plain words: when you're troubled by something, you've forgotten. And then he lists what. First, the list itself. You've forgotten that all things happen by the nature of the whole. That another person's wrong is theirs, not yours. That what's happening now has happened before and will again. That you're kin to every human being, not by blood or seed but by sharing in mind. Several reminders, every one of them something he's written earlier in these twelve books. Second, the line at the center: each person's mind, he says, is a god, and has flowed from there. The Greek word for mind is nous. For the Stoics, a divine reason runs through the whole world, and every human mind is a piece of it, a spark from the same fire. Readers take this differently. Some hear something close to religious faith. Some hear a poetic way of saying every person can reason, and so deserves respect. Marcus himself sometimes isn't sure what runs the world, as we saw a few days ago. Third, why it's in a list about being troubled. If the person who cut you off in traffic carries the same spark you do, then your anger is aimed at a relative. Not a stranger, not an enemy, a cousin in reason. That doesn't excuse what they did. It changes who you think you're dealing with. Fourth, the comfort in the word forgot. You don't need to become someone new. You need to remember what you already knew, again, which is why Marcus kept writing it down.
screen: `WHEN TROUBLED, YOU'VE FORGOTTEN.` · `EACH MIND SHARES IN THE DIVINE.` · `YOUR ANGER IS AIMED AT A RELATIVE.` · `REMEMBER, DON'T REINVENT.` · then, large: `I FORGOT.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who's been hard to deal with lately. See their face. Now try Marcus's reminder on them: this person has a mind, a spark of the same reason that's in you. They worry, they plan, they get things wrong. If you hold something sacred, you can let that word sit beside them for a moment. If you don't, just let the word kin sit there. Don't force warmth. Notice whether anything shifts. The bell holds the time.
You forgot. Marcus's line for every troubled moment: you didn't lack the truth, you dropped it, including that each person's mind shares in the divine. Today's word.
Your line: I forgot. When someone gets under your skin today, say it quietly to yourself, and look at them once as a cousin in reason. Day six hundred thirty-four.

screen: `DAY 634 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A SMALL SHARE OF TIME.`

howItsDone: Readers of the Meditations often use 12.26 as a checklist when upset, running through Marcus's reminders, among them that every person's mind shares in the same reason.

pairs: shared mind, not blood or seed

almost every reminder on the list repeats something from earlier books.
Marcus says each person's mind is a god and has flowed from there
for the Stoics, every human mind is a piece of the reason running through the world.
all readers agree on what Marcus means by the divine
some hear religious faith, some hear a way of saying every person can reason.

fork.setup: someone cuts you off in traffic and you're furious. what does 12.26 say you've forgotten?
options: that this person shares in the same reason you do.
fork.reveal: Marcus says when we're troubled we've forgotten our kinship: a community of mind, not of blood.

original.note: Greek: mind, intelligence. Marcus says each person's nous is a god, flowed from the whole.

trapdoor: what you thought: you forgot sounds like a scolding.
what it means: being troubled is a lapse of memory; the remedy is to recall what you already know.
what a scholar hears: 12.26 gathers earlier themes into one list, including the Stoic teaching that each human mind is an outflow of the divine reason that orders the cosmos.

notes: 12.26 paraphrased; confirm the reminders listed (universal nature; another's wrong; it has always happened so; kinship by intelligence not blood or seed; each mind a god and an efflux of the deity). Count deliberately left vague ('several').
Greek of 12.26: ὁ ἑκάστου νοῦς θεός καὶ ἐκεῖθεν ἐρρύηκεν. Confirm.
'Spark from the same fire' is an explanatory image, not Marcus's wording in 12.26.
The aside 'as we saw a few days ago' refers to 12.14 (day 631).
